title: Roadside warnings triggered by LAARMA slow drivers in a Queensland cassowary trial
summary: The LAARMA machine-learning system detected cassowaries with 97% recall and 77% precision, and drivers slowed by an average of 6.30 km/h and 5.06 km/h at two trial zones when its signs warned them.
account: The Large Animal Activated Roadside Monitoring and Alert System (LAARMA) was developed by the University of Sydney's Australian Centre for Robotics and CARRS-Q at the Queensland University of Technology. The developers worked with the Queensland Department of Transport and Main Roads under an iMOVE project. The system uses a machine-learning pipeline to detect large animals up to 200 m away, and it triggers roadside variable message signs. The project summary states that the system was installed in late January 2024. The consortium's iMOVE project page describes a five-month field trial: Three months of data collection came first, and two months of on-road trialing followed. The researchers report 97% recall and 77% precision. They report that drivers slowed by an average of 6.30 km/h and 5.06 km/h at two trial zones when the signs showed a warning. Their injury-risk estimates use the Nilsson model, and the research summary does not establish an observed fall in collisions. On 30 July 2025 the ABC reported that the department had used the AI for three months at a busy cassowary crossing on the Kennedy Highway at Kuranda, Far North Queensland. The ABC gave no trial dates. The department told the ABC that fatal crashes fell by 31%. About two dozen cassowaries were killed on Queensland roads the previous year. In May 2026 a department spokesperson told Mongabay that the technology shows strong potential. No wider rollout has been reported.
purpose: Detect large animals near the road in real time and warn drivers via variable message signs to reduce animal-vehicle collisions.
system: Large Animal Activated Roadside Monitoring and Alert System (LAARMA)
developer: University of Sydney Australian Centre for Robotics and QUT CARRS-Q
deployer: Queensland Department of Transport and Main Roads
taxonomy_note: The crashes cut are vehicle strikes on an endangered bird, so the gain is shared with conservation.

ratings.reason: The trial measured average vehicle speeds and modeled injury risk. No driver or bird is reported as spared in a specific event.

During the trial the Department of Transport and Main Roads had a working detector at one crossing. The developers report a recall of 0.97 and a precision of 0.77 during the on-road trial, and the department said that the equipment would be removed after the trial.

Drivers slowed by an average of 6.30 km/h and 5.06 km/h at two sites when the sign showed a warning. The department's claim of 31 percent fewer fatal crashes is not shown in the project summary, and a lower speed limit for roadwork may also have cut deaths.

ai_role.statement: The machine-learning detector decided when the roadside sign showed a warning, and the developers compared speeds with and without the warning, so the speed drops can be traced to the alerts. The 31 percent fall in fatal crashes that the department gave the ABC is not separated from other causes: a local nursery told the ABC that no deaths had occurred since the speed limit fell from 80 to 60 km/h for cyclone repair work.

fields.summary: The LAARMA machine-learning system detected cassowaries with 97% recall and 77% precision, and drivers slowed by an average of 6.30 km/h and 5.06 km/h at two trial zones when its signs warned them.
fields.account: The Large Animal Activated Roadside Monitoring and Alert System (LAARMA) was developed by the University of Sydney's Australian Centre for Robotics and CARRS-Q at the Queensland University of Technology. The developers worked with the Queensland Department of Transport and Main Roads under an iMOVE project. The system uses a machine-learning pipeline to detect large animals up to 200 m away, and it triggers roadside variable message signs. The project summary states that the system was installed in late January 2024. The consortium's iMOVE project page describes a five-month field trial: Three months of data collection came first, and two months of on-road trialing followed. The researchers report 97% recall and 77% precision. They report that drivers slowed by an average of 6.30 km/h and 5.06 km/h at two trial zones when the signs showed a warning. Their injury-risk estimates use the Nilsson model, and the research summary does not establish an observed fall in collisions. On 30 July 2025 the ABC reported that the department had used the AI for three months at a busy cassowary crossing on the Kennedy Highway at Kuranda, Far North Queensland. The ABC gave no trial dates. The department told the ABC that fatal crashes fell by 31%. About two dozen cassowaries were killed on Queensland roads the previous year. In May 2026 a department spokesperson told Mongabay that the technology shows strong potential. No wider rollout has been reported.

value.text: Detection automatically activated a warning sign. Drivers retained control of their vehicles and had to respond by slowing down and watching for cassowaries.
